summary: Specifies requirements for features to add to the IETF Datatracker so working group chairs can enter and update the status of their Internet-Drafts. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A wish list for the IETF's tracking website so chairs can update how documents are doing.

questions: how to track wg drafts in datatracker
subtitle: Features needed for IETF working group chairs to track draft document status in the Datatracker.

tldr.problem: The IETF Datatracker can track Internet-Drafts submitted to the IESG, but not drafts under development by working groups, leaving visibility gaps for WG chairs and the community about draft progression.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC specifies requirements for adding WG-level status tracking to the Datatracker, allowing chairs to input and update draft states, mark progress with annotation tags, and upload protocol writeups.
tldr.outcome: WG chairs can now track their drafts through development stages and share progress information via the Datatracker, improving visibility into the IETF standardization process.

facts.label: Scope
facts.value: WG draft status tracking in Datatracker

facts.label: Primary users
facts.value: WG Chairs, Delegates, Document Shepherds, Area Directors

today: RFC 6175 is an Informational RFC and has not been obsoleted. The requirements have been substantially implemented in the IETF Datatracker, allowing working group chairs to track and report on the status of their Internet-Drafts.

sections.title: The Datatracker and WG Draft Visibility Gap
sections.content:
The IETF Datatracker is a web-based tool for managing information about Internet-Drafts (I-Ds), RFCs, intellectual property disclosures, and liaison statements. It can track drafts that are formally submitted to the IESG (the Internet Engineering Steering Group) for publication review. However, the Datatracker has very limited ability to track the status of drafts while they are still under development by IETF working groups.

This creates a visibility problem: document authors and community members cannot easily see how WG drafts are progressing through the development process. The RFC specifies requirements to fill this gap by extending the Datatracker to allow WG chairs to input and update the status of drafts associated with their working groups.
sections.plainLanguage: The IETF uses a website to track documents becoming standards. It can track documents in the final review stage, but not documents in the working group stage. This document lists what needs to be added so chairs can update the website about their drafts.

sections.title: WG Draft States and Status Tracking
sections.content:
The Datatracker must be able to track the WG state of each draft independently from its formal IESG state. States indicate where a draft is in the working group process: whether it is being considered for adoption, already adopted, in last call, waiting for a protocol writeup, or parked. WG chairs must be able to see the current state, how long the draft has been in that state, and what the likely next states are.

Beyond the state itself, status annotation tags provide additional information about conditions affecting a draft. For example, a tag might indicate that a document needs revision, or that a Document Shepherd has started working on a protocol writeup. These tags can be used individually or in combination to describe the document's status without changing its state. The system must maintain a timestamped history of all state changes and tag updates, recording who made each change and why.
sections.plainLanguage: A draft can be in different stages: maybe the working group is thinking about adopting it, or it is already adopted and being edited, or it is waiting for someone to write a summary. The system tracks what stage it is in and what notes are attached to it.

sections.title: Access Control and Role-Based Permissions
sections.content:
The Datatracker must enforce careful access control. Everyone can read WG draft status without logging in, but only authorized people can modify it. WG chairs have full read and write privileges for all drafts in their working groups; they can change states, set annotation tags, and upload protocol writeups. Chairs can designate up to three delegates (such as WG secretaries) who receive the same privileges, even if they have other roles elsewhere in the IETF.

Document Shepherds (senior community members who review documents before IESG submission) have restricted privileges: they can only upload protocol writeups and set the 'Doc Shepherd Followup Underway' annotation tag for drafts they are assigned to. Area Directors (who oversee multiple working groups) have the same privileges as WG chairs for all groups in their area, but must be able to clearly distinguish their WG-level from their IESG-level privileges to avoid confusion.
sections.plainLanguage: The website needs to let working group chairs and their assistants update draft status, let document reviewers add their notes, and let everyone else view the information. Area directors need extra access to all the working groups they oversee.

sections.title: Protocol Writeups and Workflow Automation
sections.content:
Protocol writeups are required documents that explain a draft's technical details and design decisions to the IESG before publication. The Datatracker must make it easy to upload or input these writeups and track when they were last updated and by whom. WG chairs and Document Shepherds should be guided through the process: the system should show them which drafts need writeups and let them set the 'Doc Shepherd Followup Underway' tag to indicate work in progress.

When a protocol writeup is successfully uploaded, the Datatracker should automatically send email notifications to the draft author, WG chairs, any delegates, and the Document Shepherd. The system should also warn Document Shepherds if they try to upload a writeup before the draft reaches the 'WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup' state. Some state transitions should be automatic: for example, when a draft expires, the Datatracker should automatically move it to the 'Expired' state without requiring manual intervention.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a draft can become a standard, someone has to write an explanation for the decision makers. The website should make it easy to add that explanation and send emails when it is done. Some changes, like marking old documents as expired, should happen automatically.

sections.title: Implementation Principles and Design Approach
sections.content:
The requirements emphasize flexibility: the system should not force WG chairs to change how they work, but instead provide optional features they can use as appropriate for their situation. WG chairs might track all their drafts, some of them, or none of them in the new system, and this choice should be respected.

The implementation should reuse existing Datatracker code where practical: the user interface for WG chairs should feel similar to the interface for Area Directors updating IESG status, and the underlying system should be built as a new front-end to the existing IESG state machine. This approach reduces complexity and helps different parts of the system benefit from each other's improvements. The system must track all changes with timestamps and include information about who made each change, enabling transparency and accountability throughout the WG process.
sections.plainLanguage: The website should give chairs helpful tools but not force them to use them. It should be designed to feel familiar to chairs who already use the site, and should keep a detailed history of every change for transparency.
